summary: A notice from Alex McKenzie at BBN that Vint Cerf's UCLA group would run heavy-traffic performance experiments on the network on May 8, 1972. These could lock up the network so that no traffic flows, a problem the upcoming new IMP software was meant to prevent. Sites were advised not to schedule important network work that day.

plainLanguage.summary: Some people will test what happens when the road is jammed with lots of cars, and the road might get stuck. So everyone is told not to plan an important trip that day.

subtitle: A warning that network performance tests might cause temporary outage

tldr.problem: Researchers needed to test how the ARPANET would perform under extremely heavy traffic to a single site before new software was deployed that would prevent lockup.
tldr.mechanism: Vint Cerf's group at UCLA's Network Measurement Center scheduled performance experiments for May 8, 1972, that could potentially cause the entire network to lock up with no traffic flowing.
tldr.outcome: All ARPANET sites were warned not to schedule important network operations on May 8 due to the risk of complete network outage during the experiments.

today: RFC 334 documents early ARPANET performance testing and illustrates how the nascent network community had to carefully schedule experiments to avoid disrupting service. Today, large-scale network testing typically happens in controlled environments rather than on the production network during specified windows.

sections.title: The May 8 Performance Tests
sections.content: On May 1, 1972, Alex McKenzie of BBN announced that Vint Cerf's Network Measurement Center group at UCLA would conduct critical performance experiments on the ARPANET on Monday, May 8, 1972. These experiments were designed to measure how the network would perform under heavy traffic concentrated at a single destination site.
sections.plainLanguage: Vint Cerf's team at UCLA planned to test what happens when lots and lots of messages go to one computer at the same time.

sections.title: The Risk
sections.content: The experiments could potentially cause the network to lock up such that no traffic could flow in any direction. This problem—where the network's finite buffers fill up and prevent any progress—was exactly what the new IMPSYS 2600 software (scheduled for release on May 15) was designed to prevent. Despite the risk of complete outage, ARPA regarded these experiments as extremely important to understanding network behavior before the software deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: The test might break the network completely, but the government thought the test was important to do before putting in the new software.

sections.title: Recommendation to Sites
sections.content: BBN recommended that all ARPANET sites refrain from scheduling important network work on May 8. The announcement acknowledged the lateness of the notice and apologized for the short notice, as the experiments had just been scheduled. Sites were expected to understand that despite the disruption risk, the research was essential for understanding and improving ARPANET reliability.
sections.plainLanguage: Sites were told: don't do anything important on the network that day. BBN said sorry for telling them at the last minute.
